extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning about the procedures and powers of the U.S. House of Representatives
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of the rules, customs, powers, and practical working methods of the U.S. House of Representatives, focusing on membership qualifications, daily procedure, debate control, voting methods, committee practice, and the Speaker's powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — prohibition on military/naval officers and civil servants
rubrics_metrics.description: No military or naval officer, and no person in the civil service of the United States, can sit in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an absolute prohibition; residence in Washington also makes active private practice difficult for lawyers and businessmen, which affects who actually sits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive powers of the House
rubrics_metrics.description: The House has the exclusive right of initiating revenue bills and of impeaching officials, and chooses the President if no absolute majority of presidential electors exists for any one candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers are derived from State Constitutions and the English House of Commons; the presidential selection power was exercised in 1801 and 1825.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional sessions and bill expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Congress has two sessions (First/Long and Second/Short). Bills run on from the long session to the short session but all bills not passed by the 4th of March perish because the session is fixed by statute and cannot be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long session begins in the fall after election and continues until July/August; short session begins in December and lasts until March 4th. The fixed session calendar creates a 'terrible scramble' at the end of a Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: House meeting hours and extraordinary sittings
rubrics_metrics.description: The House usually meets at noon and sits till four or six o'clock, though hours lengthen near the close of a session; occasionally it sits all night when obstruction or urgent inter-branch messages require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices vary with the calendar and obstruction; snowstorms and other factors have led to proposals to change inauguration dates to later in March/April.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or affirmation of fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: All members (and certain officers such as the clerk, sergeant-at-arms, door-keeper, and post-master) take an oath or affirmation of fidelity to the U.S. Constitution in the form prescribed by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath is administered by the Speaker; the full text of the oath is provided in the passage and is presented as a constitutional requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sergeant-at-arms duties and mace custody
rubrics_metrics.description: The sergeant-at-arms is the treasurer of the House, pays salaries and mileage, has custody of the mace, and is responsible for keeping order (including using the mace in extreme disorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mace's design and symbolism (Roman fasces, ebony, silver bands, silver globe with eagle) are described; the sergeant's role combines administrative and enforcement functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily prayers and chaplain appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings each day begin with prayers conducted by a chaplain appointed by the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike England (where the Speaker appoints), the House appoints the chaplain and may select from any religious denomination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating allocation by lot at session start
rubrics_metrics.description: Lots are drawn for seats at the beginning of the session; each member selects a place as his turn arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of chair arrangement and the large number of members from the same state, members cannot sit in obvious party masses; this affects the drama of invective and partisan display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to remain uncovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Every member is required to remain uncovered while in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal rule of decorum analogous to older parliamentary customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of address within the House
rubrics_metrics.description: A member addresses the Speaker only and refers to another member not by name but as 'the gentleman from [State].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No use of English Commons' descriptive styles; this practice sometimes makes exact identification imperfect when many members are from one State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule forbidding passage between Speaker and member speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule (often disregarded) forbids anyone to pass between the Speaker and the member speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a curious adherence to English usage; often not strictly observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division and voting procedure (rising count, tellers, call of yeas and nays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions are taken by members rising in their seats and counted by the Speaker; if doubtful or if a count is required by one-fifth of those present (not less than one-tenth of the whole House), two tellers named by the Speaker count members as they pass between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a call of yeas and nays is demanded the clerk calls the full roll and each member answers; a second call allows those who missed the first to vote; votes may be changed between calls; the full procedure is reported in the Congressional Record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roll-call recording and restrictions on late voters
rubrics_metrics.description: Votes and lists of members not voting and of pairs are recorded in the Congressional Record; members entering after their names were passed on the second call cannot vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roll is called twice; if a member missed both, they may rise to state how they would have voted but cannot be included in the vote tally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisions as a form of obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The roll-call process can take over an hour and is an effective engine of obstruction; it can be demanded not only on substantive questions but on motions to adjourn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the procedure rests on an express constitutional provision (Art. I §5), the House cannot unilaterally abolish it; it is frequently used to waste time and force compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on speaking frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: No one may speak more than once to the same question unless he is the mover of the motion, in which case he may reply after everyone else has spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is frequently broken in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits on speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches are limited to one hour (subject to unanimous consent to extend), and in committee of the whole may be limited to five minutes; a member may yield part of his time to other members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-hour rule generally works well and does not often result in regular one-hour speeches; control of the floor (and yielding time) gives a member significant control over debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previous question (closure) — form and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The previous question is moved in the form 'Shall the main question be now put?' and when ordered it closes all debate and brings the House to an immediate vote on the main question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No debate is allowed on the motion for the previous question; it does not destroy the reporting member's right to reply; it may be moved by any member without leave and requires only a bare majority of those present. In committee its application secures five minutes to the mover of any amendment and five minutes to the first opposing speaker. It is widely used to expedite business but sometimes withheld to allow fuller discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction (filibustering) methods and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Obstruction is usually practised by repeated motions to adjourn, take a recess, or call the yeas and nays; making a speech counts as 'business' so such motions can consume hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules do not entirely prevent filibustering because of constitutional constraints and a desire to leave minority means of opposition. Two practical checks limit abuse: (1) filibustering typically needs the support of most of the minority and thus rarely succeeds unless widespread; (2) fear of popular disapproval deters excessive obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: House as committee-driven (not a debating body)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House rules through and by its committees, where discussion is unchecked by closure; the whole House mainly registers committee conclusions by vote. Only the subject of revenue receives genuine full-House discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difference distinguishes the House from a primarily debating chamber like some parliaments; committee composition therefore practically determines House action on important questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee of the whole — chairman and speaking order
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules in committee of the whole largely follow the British House of Commons, but the chairman is nominated by the Speaker on each occasion (not a permanent chairman); a rule (not always observed) forbids any member from speaking twice until every member desiring to speak has spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings in committee may be expedited by limiting discussion to a fixed period by House vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to go into secret session
rubrics_metrics.description: The House may go into secret session when confidential communications are received from the President or when a member has secret communications to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although employed in early days, this power is now in disuse; official stenographers report every word and proceedings are published in the Congressional Record, and galleries are generally left open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume and character of bills introduced, and low passage rate
rubrics_metrics.description: A very large and increasing number of bills are introduced in Congress each year (many thousands); by far the larger number are private or local bills; the proportion of bills that pass is very small (not one-thirtieth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bills are often lost by failing to reach a third reading rather than by direct rejection. Many bills are introduced to gratify particular persons or places or as political maneuvers; corporations sometimes face bills used to extort 'blackmail' and therefore maintain permanent staffs in Washington.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's powers and political role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker of the House in the U.S. has great political power: prefers his own side when recognizing speakers, decides points of order where rules are unclear (often in favor of his side), arranges business to advance or postpone bills, may refuse to recognize a member presenting a bill, advises party leaders, and nominates standing committees (selecting members and chairmen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although derived from the English model, the U.S. Speaker is expected to serve his party and exercises huge patronage through committee appointments. He must still show a measure of fairness (concede fair share of the floor, proper committee representation) and must not palpably wrest the rules; his power was reduced by rule changes around 1910 but remains significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee appointment rule (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: From January 1790 the House adopted the rule that 'All committees shall be appointed by the Speaker unless otherwise specially directed by the House.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule has been re-adopted by successive Congresses; the Speaker thereby historically selected committee memberships and chairmen, making committee composition decisive for House action. Note: rule changes (e.g., 1910) have reduced some of this power and some appointment functions now rest in a majority Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage of the title 'Honourable' for members
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the House enjoys the title of 'Honourable,' used both within the House and in the world at large (for example, in addresses of letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the title is shared with many other public officials (state senators, higher federal and state officials, judges), it is not deemed a very high distinction.
